rv.q: A Good House more than repays its international collaboration and heralds Jephta as a very bright star in the South African theatrical firmament.
Stuffed full of amazing lines, and with six super performances, essentially: A Good House is a very good play.
This isn’t perfect but it’s perceptive, provoking fun.
Amy Jephta’s incisive comedy skewers the malignant prejudices simmering within a privileged enclave in South Africa
Jephta’s highly enjoyable play has echoes of Lorraine Hansberry’s A Raisin in the Sun, Bruce Norris’s Clybourne Park and Yasmina Reza’s waspish comedies of manners.
Jephta's intriguing play would be more fulfilling with a subtler undercurrent and less underlining.

The Royal Court plays host to Amy Jephta’s South African racial proximity drama, which wastes little time in scratching away the superficial veneer of integration within a suburban enclave. We land at a cul-de-sac located within a sought-after gated development named Stillwater.
In its confident social comedy and defiantly difficult dilemmas, A Good House very much belongs on its illustrious stage.

The important issues the play raises, dramatically and occasionally amusingly, in this well-acted performance about social status and racism in an unequal society reflect particularly the current situation in South Africa, but also have relevance to wherever money grabbing neoliberals have shaped a world of cruelty around themselves.
The dynamic between the couple is ever-shifting.
But while spiky exchanges thinly veiled as neighbourliness air these uncomfortable truths, it feels unfocused, as if unsure whether it wants to be a play about racism or capitalism.
It is certainly an entertaining watch and unearths prevalent themes about xenophobia, racism and how racism often lingers in the unsaid.
A Good House is perceptive and provocative, but it’s also an imperfect mix of styles and topics.

A Good House is frustrating because South African writer Amy Jeptha's new play tantalises us with a pungent exploration of the cross section of community, class, and race but can't find the blueprints to assemble its building blocks.

Think of GOD OF CARNAGE,  CLYBOURNE PARK,  or one of the darker TV sitcoms . In such showed we expect – and here we ferociously get –  ludicrous but painful social distinctions, resentments, middle-class passive-aggression and the occasional burst of rage.

cn.t: Amy Jephta's sharp satire about race, class, and property in a South African gated community earns praise for its caustic wit and uncomfortable comedy, with critics comparing it favorably to "Clybourne Park" and applauding its raucous humor and biting social commentary.
